A prior predictive check tells you if the priors of a model give plausible
data. The `prior_pred_drm()` function draws parameters from the priors of the
dynamic range model (DRM). Then it simulates densities from these parameters.
You compare the simulated densities with the observed densities, or with what
you know about the species. One can perform this check before fitting their
models with `fit_drm()`.

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(drmr)
data(sum_fl)
```

## Simulate densities from the priors

The `prior_pred_drm()` function takes the same data, column, family, and formula
arguments as `fit_drm()`. It does not take `y_col`, because it does not use the
observed densities. The `n_draws` argument sets the number of simulated data
sets. Call `set.seed()` first to make the results reproducible.


In this example, the probability of absence depends on the number of hauls
(`c_hauls`). Recruitment depends on sea surface temperature (`c_stemp`) through
a quadratic function.

```{r}
#| label: prior-pred

set.seed(2026)
pp <- prior_pred_drm(sum_fl,
                     time_col = "year",
                     site_col = "patch",
                     n_draws = 100,
                     formula_zero = ~ 1 + c_hauls,
                     formula_rec = ~ 1 + c_stemp + I(c_stemp * c_stemp),
                     n_ages = 4)
pp
```

The printed output shows the number of draws (from the prior and prior
predictive distributions), the formulas, the data, and the parameters. The main
elements of `pp` are:

- `y_rep`: a matrix of simulated densities. It has one row for each draw and one
  column for each row of `pp$data`.
- `data`: the data, sorted by site and time. The columns of `y_rep` follow this
  order.
- `pars`: the parameter values of each draw.
- `nonfinite`: `TRUE` for each draw with `Inf`, `NaN`, or `NA` values. We may
  get `Inf`, `NaN`, or `NA` due to numeric overflow.

```{r}
#| label: dim

dim(pp$y_rep)
```

Priors with heavy tails can give extreme draws. If some draws overflow, the
function gives a warning. Remove these draws before you compare the densities:

```{r}
#| label: drop-nonfinite

y_rep <- pp$y_rep[!pp$nonfinite, , drop = FALSE]
```

## Compare the simulated and observed densities

Choose summary statistics that are important for your species. Then compare
their values in the simulated data sets with their values in the observed
data. The code below gives the proportion of zeros in each simulated data set,
and then in the observed data:

```{r}
#| label: prop-zero

summary(rowMeans(y_rep == 0))
mean(pp$data$dens == 0)
```

Also compare the scale of the densities. The code below gives quantiles of the
largest density in each simulated data set, and then the largest observed
density:

```{r}
#| label: max-dens

quantile(apply(y_rep, 1, max), probs = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))
max(pp$data$dens)
```

Use these results as follows:

- If the observed value is outside the range of the simulated values, the
  priors can exclude plausible data.
- If many simulated values are not possible for the species, the priors can be
  too wide.

## Look at the covariate effects under the priors

The `effects_drm()` function also accepts the output of `prior_pred_drm()`.  The
code below shows how recruitment changes with sea surface temperature under the
priors. The function uses the quadratic term of the formula. The band is a 90%
prior interval.

```{r}
#| label: effects

eff <- effects_drm(pp, process = "rec", variable = "c_stemp")
plot(eff)
```

Use `process = "pabs"` for the probability of absence. Use `process = "surv"`
for survival, when the model has `.toggles = list(est_surv = 1)`.

## Change the priors

Use the `.priors` argument to change a prior, as in `fit_drm()`. For the names
of the priors, see the [Model parameters and priors](model-parameters.html)
vignette. A prior for regression coefficients takes one value for all the
coefficients, or one value for each column of the design matrix.


The default prior for the recruitment coefficients is a normal distribution with
mean 0 and standard deviation 1. With a quadratic term, this prior can give very
large or very small recruitment at extreme temperatures. Moreover, the
relationship between temperature and recruitment is usually bell-shaped. Thus,
it makes sense to have the beta associated with the quadratic term negative. The
code below keeps the default prior for the intercept and the linear term. It
sets the SD to 0.5 for the quadratic term, and its mean to $-1$.
```{r}
#| label: new-priors

set.seed(2026)
pp2 <- prior_pred_drm(sum_fl,
                      time_col = "year",
                      site_col = "patch",
                      n_draws = 500,
                      formula_zero = ~ 1 + c_hauls,
                      formula_rec = ~ 1 + c_stemp + I(c_stemp * c_stemp),
                      n_ages = 4,
                      .priors = list(pr_beta_r_mu = c(0, 0, -1),
                                     pr_beta_r_sd = c(1, 1, .5)))
plot(effects_drm(pp2, process = "rec", variable = "c_stemp"))
```

When the priors pass the check, use the same priors in `fit_drm()`. Add
`y_col` to give the observed densities.
